name: Diva Blue
lede: Diva Blue is a strong purplish blue recorded on both Ridgway's 1912 chart and in Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary, with no book in our library explaining the theatrical name.

sections.title: A name two dictionaries agreed on
sections.body:
Ridgway's 1912 plate XXI gives this hue the name Diva Blue, hue 51′, tone i, and Maerz and Paul's *A Dictionary of Color* separately records it in 1930, on plate 43, row B, column 10 [1]. The ISCC-NBS system of 1955 reads the swatch as "strong blue," its block 178 [1]. *Diva* means a celebrated female singer, but neither source says whether the name honors a performer, a costume, or simply a feeling of drama; it is undocumented here [2]. A darker [[dark-diva-blue]] sits nearby on the same chart [1].

In LCH terms it measures lightness 48, chroma 41, hue 286 degrees, Munsell 7.0PB 4.8/9.8, one of the more saturated colors in this group [1]. Its closest match in the library is [[gentian-blue]], about 3.2 CIEDE2000 units away, with [[chapman-s-blue]] close behind at 3.6 units [3].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
A match within six CIEDE2000 units covering at least five percent of the canvas is rare: 38 of our 23,781 archive paintings, about 0.16 percent, as photographed [4]. It peaks in the 1910s, in 6 of 523 paintings, at 7.2 times the overall rate, and most often plays a mid-tone, in 66 percent of its appearances, with no single painter standing out against the museum baseline [4].

The earliest dated match is Fra Angelico's *Madonna of the Pomegranate*, 1426, nearly five centuries before Ridgway recorded the name in 1912; early centuries are thin in the archive, so this is a floor, not a first, and a photograph of an aged canvas is a screen color, not a pigment test [4].

origin.named_after: diva, a celebrated female singer; the specific reason is undocumented
